paras: The Kaufman County posse shooting and attempted lynching of Henry Johnson took place in Kaufman County, Texas, in May 1903, when a posse shot a Black man accused of assaulting a white farmer's wife near Kemp and a mob then tried to take him from the Kaufman jail to burn him. Officers and militia sent by the governor kept him from the mob, and within five days he was tried, sentenced to death and hanged in public at Kaufman on May 30. The case drew notice beyond Texas because the speed of the legal hanging led New York papers and a Black columnist to call it 'railroaded'.

On Monday, May 25, 1903, a Black man was accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. Whitworth, the wife of a white farmer living near Chief in Kaufman County. The Waxahachie Daily Light said the accused, whom it named John Johnson, lived on the same farm and had come to the house asking for water.

That evening a posse overtook a man near Kemp; according to a Kaufman dispatch, he refused to give his name, broke away and 'fell, riddled with bullets'. The Waxahachie paper instead described a posse of neighbors who shot him several times in a running fight and held him at Kemp until the sheriff jailed him the next morning.

On May 26 a mob at Kaufman tried to take the wounded prisoner from the jail, having formed, wire reports said, 'with the avowed purpose of burning the negro'. While wires to the town were cut, Sheriff Bill Henderson and Judge Dillard guarded the jail until militia ordered out by Governor Lanham arrived from Dallas and Terrell. The Waxahachie paper reported that a mob had hauled wood to the court house square to burn him but 'were prevailed upon not to do so'.

Johnson was tried at Kaufman on a charge of rape about May 29 and sentenced to death, while the Terrell company stood guard at the jail. He was reported to have waived appeal and the thirty days of grace, and he asked for one day before execution; other reports said he pleaded guilty or confessed.

On May 30 Sheriff Henderson hanged him in the court house yard before several thousand people, with the Terrell company holding back the crowd. During the hanging a Black man from near Kemp reportedly struck at a Whitworth brother with a knife and was pursued by a crowd; the coverage does not show what became of him.

The first white reports treated the accusation as fact and the shooting as vengeance: the Daily Ardmoreite headed its Terrell dispatch 'It's the Same Old Story' and 'Vengeance Overtakes a Vile Negro Ravisher'. The Alexandria Gazette ran a Fort Worth wire as 'Killed by Sheriff's Posse' and Shreveport's Caucasian said he was 'shot to death', claims later reports contradicted. A short wire on the militia ran as 'Threatened With Cremation' in the Arizona Republican and as troops sent 'to protect a negro' in Savannah and Atlanta.

The Texas paper the Waxahachie Daily Light followed the case daily and headed its hanging story 'Negro Rapist Executed'. The hanging wire ran in Georgia and South Carolina, and Texas and Arkansas digests noted he was 'legally hanged' within a week. The Sun of New York headed a New Orleans dispatch 'Railroaded to His Death', calling it hanging 'the Nacogdoches way' and noting that state law forbade public hangings. A New York World editorial, reprinted in Birmingham, said Johnson had 'waived' his rights 'under what persuasion or compulsion is not stated'.

A columnist in the St. Paul Appeal wrote that an 'Afro-American' had been railroaded through the courts and hanged within four days, calling this 'a little improvement upon lynching'. The Wichita Searchlight's lynching chronology listed an 'Unknown Negro, criminal assault, Kemp, Texas' among May's lynchings.

Accounts of the shooting come only from the pursuers' side: the first wires said he was shot as he ran from questioning, the St. Louis Republic after capture as he tried to escape, and the Waxahachie paper in a running fight in which he was 'unceremoniously fired on by the infuriated citizens'. One wire named the sheriff Anderson, but later reports name Bill Henderson; papers also differ on the time of capture and the husband's first name.

reader.title: Shooting and attempted lynching of Henry Johnson
bases: A posse shot the accused while pursuing him and a mob tried to take him from jail to burn him (A2, A4, A5); he was then legally hanged after a trial (A10), so the lynching was attempted, not completed.
Independent Kaufman, Terrell, Dallas and Kemp dispatches agree on the assault accusation, the posse shooting and the mob at the jail (A2, A3, A4, A7, A8).

accounts.label: Sheriff's-posse wire (Fort Worth/Kaufman)
accounts.gist: Sheriff's posse overtook the man near Kemp at 9 p.m.; when he would not give his name and ran, he was 'riddled with bullets'; first headlines said he was killed.

accounts.label: Waxahachie Daily Light (Texas)
accounts.gist: A posse of neighbors pursued him and arrested him after a running fight about 6 p.m., shooting him several times; the sheriff took him to jail the next morning; a mob hauled wood to burn him but was talked out of it.

accounts.label: Kemp dispatch
accounts.gist: Said he was 'shot to death by the posse while he was attempting to escape'.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch / New York World
accounts.gist: He was hanged legally but 'railroaded', within four days, in public against state law, after waiving appeal and 30 days of grace; the militia alone prevented a lynching.

accounts.label: Black columnist
accounts.gist: He was 'railroaded' through the courts and hanged within four days, which the writer called 'a little improvement upon lynching'.

framing.detail: Headlines 'It's the Same Old Story / Vengeance Overtakes a Vile Negro Ravisher' and 'Negro Rapist Executed' treat the accusation as fact and the shooting as vengeance.
Out-of-state papers ran short wires on the militia ('Troops Called Out to Protect a Negro', 'Threatened With Cremation') and the death sentence.

The Sun's 'Railroaded to His Death' and the World editorial accepted guilt but questioned the waived appeal, the 30 days of grace 'waived ... under what persuasion or compulsion is not stated', and the public hanging.
The St. Paul Appeal called it railroading, with irony about being 'thankful'; the Wichita Searchlight listed the case as a lynching from the early reports.

conflicts.note: The 'killed' versions are early or headline claims; later local reports and the execution show he survived the shooting.
